messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam was a 21-year-old European American man who had been married only a short time and was currently unemployed, spending much of his days at home with his wife. His difficulties began after a violent assault on his younger brother, which had happened late one evening outside a convenience store near their apartment. Liam had been walking several steps behind when two men came up quickly, one making a sudden movement toward his brother before the other struck him. He remembered the scene in fragments that felt fixed and unchangeable, as if he were looking at photographs: his brother’s arm jerking up, the flash of a hand near a sleeve, the angle of a shoulder collapsing under the blow. He could not tell the story smoothly, and when he tried, the memory fell apart into pieces. What stayed with him most vividly were sensory scraps — the sharp, metallic smell of blood mixed with the pavement and the stale air near the store entrance — and these would surface later with no warning, as if his mind had returned him to that same sidewalk.

Afterward, Liam began to notice that anything that reminded him of that night pulled him apart quickly. If people in a parking lot looked suspicious, if someone glanced too long toward him and his wife, if relatives made remarks about family being “protective” or “strong,” or if he caught sight of a forearm, a swollen knuckle, or another body part that echoed the assault, he would tense immediately and steer away. Those moments drove him to watch less television and avoid films or news stories about attacks, and he started refusing to stay alone in a room or building, insisting on sitting close to his wife or calling someone until he felt less exposed. Sudden movements by others put him instantly on guard; even a neighbor reaching into a bag too quickly could make his whole body brace. He would lie awake after such encounters, replaying the night over and over, and the more he tried to shut the images out, the more they came back in the same fixed, photographic form. Sometimes the smell would return too, and with it the sense that the event was not over.

Liam had come to believe that his body was betraying him, reacting as if danger were still present even when he was safe in his own apartment. He felt he was no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him, and he had started to doubt that he could rely on himself to stay composed or protect the people he loved. Those beliefs made him scan for trouble constantly, and that vigilance sharpened his reactions to the very cues he feared most: suspicious faces, family-related comments, and any sudden motion could set off the same alarm. Once aroused, he became even more convinced that he was unsafe, and the fear fed directly into the habits he had built to get through the day. He avoided being alone, which kept him from settling long enough to prove to himself that a quiet room was tolerable. He watched less media and filled his evenings with whatever he could get through beside his wife, partly to keep the images away and partly because silence gave the memory room to intrude. When the pressure became unbearable, he had hurt himself physically just to release the overwhelming feelings, and for a few minutes the pain had cut through the panic. But afterward he felt more shaken, more ashamed, and even less able to trust his own responses.

Over time, those strategies seemed to help only in the moment and left Liam more stuck with the memory. He noticed that avoiding reminders did not erase them; it narrowed his world until more ordinary things — a comment from a cousin, a stranger’s quick gesture, the sight of an arm or hand in a certain position — felt newly dangerous. The less he spoke about what happened, the less he could organize it into words, and the memory stayed in its fragmented, sensory form. That silence also fed the feeling that he was weak and unreliable, as if his inability to explain the assault proved that he had failed in some essential way. By the time he came for help, his sleep was badly disrupted, he was spending much of his time on edge, and he had started to worry that he was becoming a burden to his wife. What finally brought him to seek treatment was the fear that the cycle was tightening again after another evening of suddenly feeling as if the attack were happening in the room with him, and what he most hoped for was to feel steady enough to be alone without panic and to trust that his body would stop sounding the alarm when nothing was there.
